title: Stoic in grief
hook: honest grief, the seasons, sweet memory

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was oikeiōsis, the household as the hive and your first circle. Your line was for the house.

Someone at the funeral says it to the dead man's daughter, meaning well: you're being so strong. She hasn't cried in front of anyone. She went back to work on Monday. People admire it. And at two in the morning, alone in her kitchen, it isn't strength at all. It's a held breath. That's the common picture of Stoic grief: a stiff upper lip, nothing shown. Seneca's letters paint a different one.
screen: `YOU'RE BEING SO STRONG.` → `TWO A.M., A HELD BREATH.` → `WHAT SENECA'S GRIEF LOOKS LIKE.`

segments.voice: Three threads, held together. First, honest grief. Seneca, writing to Lucilius after a friend's death, doesn't tell him not to cry. The eyes shouldn't be dry when a friend is lost, he says, nor should they overflow: tears are allowed, wailing isn't required. Then he confesses that when his own friend Annaeus Serenus died, he wept beyond all measure, and counts himself among those whom grief defeated. A teacher who admits that is not asking for stone. Second, the seasons. The Stoics placed death inside nature's turning, like the ripe olive. That doesn't cancel sorrow. It's a frame big enough to hold it: leaves fall, and you still miss the green. Seneca, writing to a mother three years into mourning her son, is gentle and patient, and also asks her, slowly, to let her life go on. Third, sweet memory. Seneca passes on a saying from his teacher Attalus: remembering lost friends can be pleasant, the way some fruits are good because they're a little sharp, or a very old wine has a bitterness that pleases. Seneca's hope is that the memory of those we've lost becomes a joy, not only a wound. Put together: tears when they come, a loss held inside the turning year, and, over time, the person coming back as a memory you can visit with something like gladness. Not instead of sorrow. Alongside it. And today closes a week of carrying the porch into ordinary days.
screen: `EYES NOT DRY, NOT OVERFLOWING.` · `SENECA WEPT BEYOND MEASURE.` · `A FRAME BIG ENOUGH FOR SORROW.` · `MEMORY, SHARP AND SWEET.` · then, large: `GRIEF, HONESTLY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one loss, a person, an animal, a place, a time of life, choosing one that feels bearable today; you don't have to open the hardest door. Let yourself feel what's there, honestly, then let one specific memory come, a voice, a joke, a meal, and hold it like a sharp, sweet fruit. If tears come, they're welcome here; if they don't, that's fine too.
Attalus, the teacher whose saying Seneca passed on: that remembering lost friends can turn sweet, like a good bitterness, over time. Today's word.
Your line: grief, honestly. Tears and gladness can share the same memory. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some readers of Seneca treat grief as something to feel honestly rather than suppress, and over time to turn into grateful memory of the person lost.

Seneca.meaning: a Roman Stoic writer whose letters to Lucilius discuss grief

Lucilius.meaning: Seneca's younger friend, to whom he wrote his moral letters

Annaeus Serenus.meaning: Seneca's friend, whose death made him weep beyond measure

Attalus.meaning: Seneca's teacher, who said memory of lost friends can be sweet

notes: Letters 63 paraphrased: eyes neither dry nor overflowing (63.1); Attalus on memory of lost friends like fruits with an agreeable sharpness and old wine's bitterness (63.5); let the recollection become pleasant (63.7); Seneca's confession about Annaeus Serenus (63.14). Confirm.
Consolation to Marcia: Marcia mourning her son Metilius for three years. Confirm.
